correctness.rationale: The collision formula is reconstructed from exact fiber counting in all characteristics other than 2,3. It implies a four-term nonnegative global deficit after square completion and phase/pair inequalities. Expanding the exact quartic around the normalized positive extremizer gives quadratic coefficients 24/(2q+1), 4-8/(2q+1) and 4, each on an m-dimensional orthogonal sector; radial and extremizer tangents exhaust the kernel. Uniform smooth tubular expansion and an explicit weakest-mode perturbation prove the exact local distance coefficient. Package checker symbolically replays Hessian polynomials at q=5,7,11 and independently checks modular collision fibers and the deficit at 36 deterministic inputs; these finite checks only corroborate the universal proof.

originality.rationale: The earlier public cubic-graph theorem (published-finding corpus ID 2db777d1e47b) determines the exact extension norm and equality class and gives the quartic collision formula, but its inspected full proof does not compute the new global nonnegative four-term deficit, the complete three positive second-variation levels and their kernels, or the sharp local squared-distance coefficient 24/(2q+1). The 2024 primary paper treats other surfaces and moments; the 2019 integer-cubic-curve paper concerns tenth moments. The added result is perturbative and quantitative rather than reassertion of the sharp norm. Searches for exact Hessian spectra and equivalent stability coefficients returned no covering result. Historical priority remains provisional.
residual_risks: A broader unpublished or unindexed quantitative extremizer-stability theorem could yield the same curvature spectrum.

value.rationale: The exact local curvature and q-dependent least-band decay quantify near-extremizer rigidity for an intrinsically resonant cubic Fourier curve. This gives an analytic stability classification with three distinct amplitude/phase channels and a sharp perturbative constant, not merely the previously known sharp norm or equality case. It identifies why near-extremizer inverse statements become weaker as field size increases; the result is complete for the fixed-field local problem.
